1. The animation shows a grid of cells, one for each historical starting month. Light cells are months where a buyer was ahead after ten years. Dark cells are months where a renter was ahead. It compares buying with renting using US home prices (FHFA), rents (BLS) and mortgage rates (Freddie Mac). It is labeled "illustrative" and "history, not a forecast."

2. The dark band in the middle of the grid shifts and changes shape across frames 1–3. A few cells at the left edge and at the right edge change too. In frames 4–6 a caption appears: "rent tag 4%: buyer ahead in 64.2% of start months." The grid stays almost the same from frame to frame. The caption is the main addition.

3. The meaning is that, under an assumed 4% rent-growth tag, buying came out ahead after ten years in about 64% of historical start months. Renting came out ahead in the other 36% or so. The dark band suggests renting won for people who started in one particular stretch of years. So buying won more often, but not always, and the result depended on when you started.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that buying has more often paid off over a ten-year hold, but that timing matters and the result isn't guaranteed.

5. The advice in 4 is my own conclusion. The on-screen text only reports the 64.2% figure and warns that it is history and not a forecast. It never tells the viewer to buy or rent.
